p: Offload: the time from an ambulance arriving at an emergency room until the hospital takes over the patient.
90th percentile: nine out of ten handoffs were faster than this time.
Local target: set by each local EMS agency. In San Bernardino County the Inland Counties EMS Agency target is 25 minutes. California's AB 40 push is for no more than 30 minutes, met 90% of the time.
Lower bound: the true figure is at least this, and probably higher.

By definition of a 90th percentile, at least 10% of a month's handoffs took the 90th-percentile time or longer. Each of those exceeded the target by at least the gap between the two. So the stuck time is at least:
hours = 0.10 x N x (P90 - S) / 60
N is the number of handoffs, P90 is the 90th-percentile time in minutes, S is the local target in minutes. If P90 is not above S the result is 0, which does not mean there was no delay.
Example, January 2026, Community Hospital of San Bernardino: N = 653, P90 = 43:35, S = 25. That gives about 20.2 hours.
Green: at least 90% of handoffs met the target. Yellow: 75% to 89.9%. Red: below 75%. Every color is paired with a word and a shape.

EMSA publishes only hospitals whose 90th percentile was above their local target and that had at least 60 handoffs. Every hospital in the report therefore has fewer than 90% on target, so green never appears for a listed hospital in this data. A hospital missing from a month is shown gray as Not listed because the report does not say whether it met the target, had too few handoffs, or did not report.

methods.sections.h: What the numbers do not mean
p: Offload time measures crowding at handoff, not the quality of care. Critical patients are usually seen quickly. The main harm is that ambulances are unavailable for the next call.
The 90th percentile hides how long the longest waits were. The what-if slider is a scenario using the lower-bound formula, not a prediction of response times or lives saved.
The app never ranks hospitals as good or poor and never tells anyone where to go for care.

We train on earlier months and test on the most recent two, never at random. Baseline A assumes nothing changes. Baseline B continues a short trend. A logistic regression and a ridge regression are the experimental models. If they do not beat the baselines the app says so. See the Forecast page for the current result.

California EMS Authority (EMSA), monthly APOT exceedance reports to the Commission on EMS, September 2025 to February 2026 data. Note that EMSA names each file by the month it was posted, so the file titled with one month usually holds the previous month's data. The app reads the data month from inside each report.
Hospital locations, trauma designations and health centers: California Department of Public Health licensed and certified healthcare facility listing (data.chhs.ca.gov).
District boundaries: U.S. Census Bureau cartographic boundary file, 119th Congress. ZIP code centers: Census ZCTA gazetteer.
Map tiles when online: OpenStreetMap contributors. Map library: Leaflet.
Reports are monthly, so the app shows typical conditions, not live ones.
The newest EMSA report found was posted in March 2026 (February 2026 data). Later months may exist; the app checks for new reports monthly and says when its data is out of date.

Arrowhead Regional Medical Center and other hospitals do not appear in the reports we have. Per the report's own rules that means the target was met, fewer than 60 handoffs were recorded, or data was not reported.
Two reports state one more exceeding hospital in their text than their tables list (December 2025: 163 stated, 162 listed; February 2026: 161 stated, 160 listed). We use the tables.
The September 2025 report has no table, and its data month has no handoff-percentage column. No data is shown for hospitals before September 2025.

Some hospitals could not be matched to a map location and are shown in lists only. Hospital locations come from a public facility list and were matched by name; matches that were not clearly the same hospital were left unplaced rather than guessed.
Redlands Community Hospital and Loma Linda University Medical Center are inside district CA-23, not CA-33, by the Census boundary.

No accounts, no sign-in, no cookies, no analytics. ZIP code and city searches happen in your browser. If you type a street address, your browser sends that text to OpenStreetMap Nominatim to find its location. Nothing is sent to us. The chosen language is saved only in your own browser. If you tap Drive time, your browser sends the start and end points to OpenStreetMap's public routing server (routing.openstreetmap.de) to get the route.
Hospitals, agencies and residents can report a data error through the project's issue page.

about.lead: OffloadWatch shows where ambulances get stuck waiting at hospitals and predicts where it may get worse, so residents, officials and EMS crews can see the problem and act on it.
about.who: Built by Palash Rakshit for the Congressional App Challenge.
about.why: California's AB 40 push is for each local EMS agency to adopt an ambulance offload standard of no more than 30 minutes, met 90% of the time. The Inland Counties EMS Agency standard is 25 minutes. In January 2026 the slowest 10% of handoffs at Community Hospital of San Bernardino took 43 minutes 35 seconds or longer, and 66.6% of its handoffs met the standard. Statewide, the state publishes this in monthly PDFs. Some counties, such as San Diego, Orange, Alameda and Sacramento, publish their own dashboards. OffloadWatch adds a statewide view and the congressional-district view, and a way to act on the numbers.
about.modes: Residents: type an address or ZIP code, see nearby hospitals and how crowded handoffs usually are, with a 911 reminder and nearby health centers. English and Spanish.
Officials: a printable one-page district report card with lower-bound ambulance-hours and a what-if slider.
Analysts: a next-month outlook tested against simple baselines, downloads and a methods page.
about.tools: Data pipeline in Python (pdfplumber, pandas, scikit-learn, shapely). Website in plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript with Leaflet for maps. Map data from OpenStreetMap contributors, the U.S. Census Bureau and the California Department of Public Health. This project was built with the help of an AI coding assistant (Claude Code from Anthropic); the contest rules on AI-assisted code apply and this note is here so that use is stated openly.

ps.problem: When an ambulance reaches a crowded ER, the crew waits for the hospital to take over the patient. While they wait, that ambulance can't answer the next 911 call. Statewide this is reported mainly in monthly PDFs sent to a state commission. Some counties publish their own dashboards; I found no tool that shows it by congressional district.
ps.solution: It puts those reports on a map, shows how long handoffs take at each hospital, adds up the ambulance-hours stuck (a minimum), and tests whether next month can be predicted. Free, no sign-in, English and Spanish.

act.protocol: EMSA tells every hospital on its list to carry out a plan to reduce ambulance waits. You can ask to see that plan.
act.letter.district:
Hello,

I am a resident writing about ambulance wait times at hospitals in {place}.

According to the California EMS Authority's {month} report, ambulances lost at least {hours} hours waiting to hand off patients at hospitals in {place}. At {worst}, nine out of ten handoffs took less than {p90} minutes, against a {std}-minute target. Every hour an ambulance waits is an hour it cannot answer a 911 call.

Could you tell me what is being done to bring these waits down, and by when? EMSA tells hospitals over their target to carry out an offload-reduction plan. I would like to know whether that plan is working here.

Source: California EMS Authority monthly APOT exceedance reports (emsa.ca.gov/apot). The figures are monthly minimums.

Thank you,
[Your name]
